title: Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement Method
summary: Standardizes one variant of Diffie-Hellman key agreement, based on a draft from the ANSI X9F1 working group. Two parties can use it to arrive at a shared secret over an open channel.

eli5.summary: Two friends mix their secret colors into a shared paint bucket in public. They each end up with the same final color, and nobody watching can work it out.

questions: what is a small subgroup attack
how is a kek derived from diffie-hellman
subtitle: How two parties use Diffie-Hellman to agree on a secret and turn it into keying material for encrypting a message.

tldr.problem: Two parties who have not shared a secret in advance need a way to agree on a symmetric key over an open channel, and the many variants of Diffie-Hellman needed one standardized form.
tldr.mechanism: Each side combines its own private key with the other's public key to compute the same shared number ZZ. A SHA-1 based function then turns ZZ plus some context into as much keying material as needed, typically a key-encryption key.
tldr.outcome: Ephemeral-Static mode MUST be implemented and Static-Static mode is optional. The security rests entirely on keeping private keys secret, and static keys need protection against small subgroup attacks.

today: RFC 2631 is a Proposed Standard and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What the RFC Standardizes
sections.content:
Diffie and Hellman described a way for two parties to agree on a shared secret that eavesdroppers cannot learn. A large number of minor variants of the process exist. RFC 2631 standardizes one of them, based on the ANSI X9.42 draft from the ANSI X9F1 working group.

The shared secret is then converted into keying material for symmetric algorithms. Typically that material is used as a key-encryption key (KEK) to wrap a content-encryption key (CEK), which in turn encrypts the message data. The variant requires the recipient to have a certificate. The originator may have a static key pair, with its public key in a certificate, or an ephemeral key pair.
sections.eli5: Two friends want a secret code word without ever whispering it. This document explains one exact recipe for doing that, so everybody follows the same steps.

sections.title: Computing the Shared Secret ZZ
sections.content:
Both parties have key pairs. The shared secret, called ZZ, is defined as ZZ = g ^ (xb * xa) mod p. In practice each side computes ZZ = (yb ^ xa) mod p = (ya ^ xb) mod p, using its own private key and the other's public key.

Here xa and xb are the private keys, ya = g ^ xa mod p and yb = g ^ xb mod p are the public keys, p and q are large primes, and g has order q modulo p. The value j is a large integer such that p = qj + 1.

In the Cryptographic Message Syntax (RFC 2630), the recipient's key is identified through its certificate. The sender's public key is identified either by reference to its certificate or by inline inclusion.
sections.eli5: Each friend keeps one secret number and shares a scrambled version of it. Mixing your own secret with the other's scrambled number gives both of you the very same answer.

sections.title: Turning ZZ into Keying Material
sections.content:
The RFC derives an arbitrary amount of keying material from ZZ with KM = H ( ZZ || OtherInfo ), where H is SHA-1. Leading zeros of ZZ MUST be preserved, so ZZ occupies as many octets as p. For a 1024-bit p, ZZ is 128 bytes.

OtherInfo is a DER-encoded structure with three parts. The keyInfo holds the object identifier of the key-wrap algorithm and a 4-byte counter, which starts at 1 and goes up by one each time the function runs for a given KEK. The optional partyAInfo is a random string from the sender, and if present it MUST contain 512 bits. The suppPubInfo is the length of the generated KEK in bits, as a 32-bit number in network byte order.

To build a KEK, generate one or more KM blocks, incrementing the counter, and concatenate them left to right. The KEK is the left-most n bytes of KM. For 3-key 3DES (192 bits) the function runs twice, then the pieces are parity adjusted. RC2-128 needs one run and RC2-40 also needs one.

The only secret entropy is ZZ, so the effective KEK key space is limited by the size of ZZ even if a longer string is generated.
sections.eli5: The shared answer is like a seed. A fixed blender recipe turns the seed, plus a few labels, into as long a key as you need, one batch at a time.

sections.title: Key and Parameter Requirements
sections.content:
The group parameters must have the form p = jq + 1 where q is a large prime and j is at least 2. A private key x must be in the interval [2, q - 2] and should be chosen randomly, and the public key is y = g^x mod p. To comply with this memo, q MUST be at least 160 bits long, and p must be a minimum of 512 bits. A larger q may be advisable with symmetric ciphers stronger than DES.

Agents SHOULD generate the domain parameters (g, p, q) with the algorithm in the RFC, derived from FIPS 186 and X9.42. It picks a SEED, builds q from SHA-1 outputs, and tests for primality with a test where a non-prime passes with probability at most 2^-80. It then searches for p and finally picks g by raising a trial value h to the power (p-1)/q until g is not 1.

Recipients may check the parameters using the j and validationParms elements in the PKIX key syntax, by verifying p = qj + 1 and re-running the generation procedure with the stated seed. Whether agents give this validation information in their certificates is a local matter between agents and their CA.
sections.eli5: The recipe needs big special numbers. The document says how big they must be and gives a careful way to find them so that no one can sneak in a weak one.

sections.title: Ephemeral-Static and Static-Static Modes
sections.content:
In Ephemeral-Static mode the recipient has a static, certified key pair, and the sender generates a new key pair for each message and sends the public part. Because ZZ then differs for every message, partyAInfo MAY be omitted. If the same ephemeral key is reused, for example cached for performance, a separate partyAInfo MUST be used for each message. All implementations MUST implement this mode.

In Static-Static mode both sides have static certified key pairs. ZZ is then the same for each message, so partyAInfo MUST be used, and different for each message, to give each message a different KEK. Implementations MAY implement this mode.

Public key validation is described as an optional check: the key y must lie in the interval [2, p-1], and y^q mod p must equal 1. Its main purpose is to prevent a small subgroup attack. In Ephemeral-Static mode the recipient SHOULD do the check, though it MAY skip it if an opponent cannot tell whether decryption succeeded. In Static-Static mode both sides SHOULD either validate or verify that the CA has checked the key. The RFC notes that this procedure may be subject to pending patents.
sections.eli5: In one mode the sender makes a brand-new secret for every message. In the other, both people reuse their long-term secrets, so they add a fresh random label each time to keep the messages from sharing a key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security comes from the secrecy of the private keys. If either private key is disclosed, all messages sent or received using it are compromised, and losing a private key means being unable to read messages sent to it.

Static Diffie-Hellman keys are vulnerable to a small subgroup attack. In practice this affects both sides in Static-Static mode and the receiver in Ephemeral-Static mode. The validation steps in the mode descriptions guard against it, and keys can alternatively be generated so that they resist it.

The security level depends on three things: the symmetric key length (about 2^l for l bits), the size of q (a 2^(m/2) level) and the size of p (a subexponential level). A balanced design makes all three about equal, and overall security is limited by the lowest.
sections.eli5: The whole trick is only safe if your secret number stays secret. Also, certain reused secrets can be tricked out of you, so you should check what you are given.
